opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that most current LLM-based approaches don't really have a native way of representing a sequence of visual frames. They borrow the language paradigm and force video into it.

The typical pipeline is: take a pretrained vision encoder, often something CLIP-like, chop each frame into patches, turn those into tokens, maybe compress or pool them, and then concatenate everything into one long sequence that the language model reads as if it were text. Time becomes just another position index. A video becomes a very long, very redundant sentence.

That works surprisingly well for some things. You can do captioning, answer questions about what happened, retrieve moments. But I think it hides some fundamental problems.

First, the representation is mostly semantic and language-aligned. Encoders like CLIP are trained to match images with captions, so they keep what's nameable, like "a dog," "a kitchen," "someone running," and throw away a lot of what isn't easily described in words: precise geometry, physical dynamics, fine spatial relationships, how things persist and change over time. And those are exactly the things you need if you want a model that understands the physical world.

Second, there's an efficiency mismatch. Language is already a highly compressed, human-designed signal. Every token carries a lot of meaning. Visual frames are the opposite: dense, continuous, highly redundant. Neighboring frames are almost identical. If you treat every patch of every frame as a token, the context explodes, so people end up subsampling frames or aggressively pooling tokens. Then the model is effectively looking at a slideshow, not a continuous stream. You lose the temporal continuity that makes video video.

Third, and I think this is the deepest issue, the language model sits at the center, and vision is treated as an input adapter. The reasoning, the "world model," lives in the language space. Vision gets translated into something the LLM can digest. I'm not convinced that's the right long-term architecture. Humans and animals build very rich models of space, objects and causality long before language, and a lot of that understanding is never verbalized.

So my view is that the current approach is a useful engineering shortcut, but it's not a real solution for visual intelligence. What I'd like to see is visual representations that are learned more from the visual signal itself, through self-supervision, prediction, maybe generative modeling, so they capture structure, spatial relations and temporal dynamics. Then you'd have some kind of persistent memory or state that evolves over time, rather than just stacking tokens in a context window. Language should connect to that, but it shouldn't be the bottleneck everything has to squeeze through.

In short: today video is read like text. I think eventually we need models that actually see and remember, in a way closer to how a spatial, embodied intelligence experiences the world.

r001.rationale: The response says frame patches are turned into tokens and “concatenate[d] ... into one long sequence” for the language model to read.

fable-5.1.text:
Right now, honestly, most LLM-based systems treat a video as a bag of image tokens with a timestamp stapled on. You take each frame, run it through a vision encoder like CLIP or SigLIP, get a few hundred patch tokens, maybe pool them down, and then you just concatenate them in order and hand the whole thing to the language model. The temporal structure is almost entirely delegated to the LLM's positional encoding and attention. So the model "knows" frame 3 came after frame 2 the same way it knows one word came after another.

That works surprisingly well for a lot of benchmarks, which is part of the problem. Many video QA tasks can be solved from one or two frames, so the representation never gets pressured to actually model motion, causality, or what persists across time. What the model learns is closer to "describe this set of images and guess the story" than real spatiotemporal understanding.

There are a few things I think are missing. First, the encoder is still fundamentally an image encoder. Very little of the visual pretraining is about dynamics, about how things move and interact. Second, the token budget is brutal. If you sample sparsely you lose the fine temporal signal, if you sample densely you blow up the context, and the compression schemes people use, pooling, token merging, Q-Former style resamplers, tend to be designed to preserve what helps language modeling, not what helps physical understanding. Third, everything is being forced through the bottleneck of language. The representation is shaped by whether it helps predict the next text token, and a lot of what makes video rich, continuous geometry, intuitive physics, just does not compress well into words.

So my view is that the current approach is a pragmatic engineering solution that borrows the LLM's sequence machinery, but it is not yet a representation of video in any deep sense. The direction I am more excited about is building visual world representations that are learned from video itself, with their own notion of state and time, and then having language sit on top of that rather than being the backbone everything gets squeezed through.

r001.rationale: The candidate says systems encode each frame into patch tokens and “concatenate them in order” before passing the sequence to the language model.

astra-6.text:
I think the current approach is essentially to turn video into a very long sequence of tokens. You take a frame, encode it into visual tokens, then do the same for the next frame, and concatenate those tokens for the language model to process. You can add positional information or timestamps so the model knows their order.

That gives you a representation of a sequence of images, but it doesn’t necessarily give you a good representation of motion or how the world evolves. A lot of information is repeated across neighboring frames, yet you’re spending tokens encoding it again. And if you sample frames sparsely to keep the sequence manageable, you can miss what happens between them.

So I would distinguish being able to describe a video from learning a useful temporal representation. The model may infer what happened from a few snapshots, which can be very powerful. But that alone doesn’t tell us whether it has captured the underlying dynamics. I think that’s an important question for these approaches.

r001.rationale: The response says each frame is encoded into visual tokens and those tokens are concatenated for the language model to process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between representing individual frames and representing what happens across frames. In a typical LLM-based approach, you encode each frame into visual tokens, concatenate those tokens in temporal order, and let the language model reason over the sequence. So you have a sequence of spatial representations, with some indication of time.

That can work well for describing a clip or answering questions about it. But putting frames in order doesn’t automatically give you a representation of motion or dynamics. How does an object persist? What changed between two frames? What caused that change? The model has to infer those relationships from the tokens.

So the question for me is whether this representation captures the underlying temporal structure, or whether it mostly captures a collection of snapshots that the language model can connect. Those are related capabilities, but they’re not the same.

r001.rationale: The response says each frame is encoded into visual tokens and those tokens are concatenated in temporal order, forming a sequence.
